title: Pioneers of Contemporary Indian Art
summary: At the beginning of the 19th century, under British rule, Indian art declined; the craft and technique of fresco and miniature painting were nearly lost and miniatures were ousted by European oil painting (the Company School). Towards the turn of the century traditional Indian painting faded out and Indian artists began to look at their heritage positively. Raja Ravi Varma of Kerala was famous for mythological subjects and portraiture with western influence in oil paintings. Abanindranath Tagore tried to recreate a new style; Nandalal Bose, Benode Behari and others followed this nationalism and the Bengal School emerged in the first half of the 20th century (centre: Santiniketan). They took inspiration from Indian classics and mythology, rejected western realism for the idealism of Indian art and used traditional watercolour techniques with Indian and Chinese styles, inspired by miniatures, frescoes and folk art. Jamini Roy gave a modern form to folk art and Rabindranath Tagore introduced expression into painting. Amrita Shergil drew on both Western and Indian traditions and is the first lady of modern Indian art. The Bengal School provided the starting point of contemporary Indian art.

Artist: Raja Ravi Varma (born in the village of Kilimanoor, Kerala; died 2 October 1906). Medium: oil on canvas. Date: 1899. He was a prominent representative of the Europeanised school, famous for water and oil colour techniques and for the vast panorama of Indian mythology with heroines as central figures (Dushyanta–Shakuntala, Nala–Damayanti, the Mahabharata); his paintings of divinities survive in prints, calendars, posters and oleographs. 'Hamsa Damayanti' created a sensation at the Madras Fine Arts Exhibition. Damayanti, the most beautiful of his women, shapely and graceful in a red sari, lovingly listens to the messages of her lover Nala narrated by the swan (hamsa); the silent love shows in the sparkle of her eyes and the glow of her cheeks. Ravi Varma provided the vital link between traditional Indian art (the Thanjavur school) and Western academic realism, and is also considered a great patriot.

Artist: Amrita Shergil (born 1913; father Sardar Umrao Singh Shergil, Hungarian mother Lady Antoinette). Medium: oil on canvas. Date: 1938. Collection: National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi. She spent her early years in Europe and studied in Paris, and was influenced by the Post-Impressionists including Modigliani and Gauguin. She came to India in 1921 and drew inspiration from Kangra miniatures and Ajanta frescoes; a visit to South India inspired 'The Bride's Toilette', 'The Brahmacharies' and 'South Indian Villagers Going to Market'. 'Brahmacharies' shows five male figures, young Brahmin students in an ashram, as symbols of devotion in the Hindu faith. It is composed on a horizontal plane with vertical placement of figures; there is a variety of colour of the bodies; the deep red background, white dhotis (subtle variations of white) and a neutral greenish-grey foreground keep the composition calm; the off-white of the central figure with black and brown bodies around stands out against the red. She painted for just seven years; she was the youngest and most short-lived of the pioneers, and her paintings have a quality of timelessness.

Artist: Gaganendranath Tagore (born 1867 in Kolkata; died 1938). Medium: water colour on paper. Date: 1920. Size: 12.5 x 9.5 inches. Collection: Rabindra Bharati Society, Jorasanko, Kolkata. His important works of 1910–21 were sketches of the Himalayas, the life of Chaitanya in sequence and drawings of Indian life. He supported his brother Abanindranath but also inclined towards the Cubist school of Europe and developed his own brand of cubism with overlapping, flattened geometrical shapes of colour that create a mysterious world, with a dramatic play of light and shade; he never blindly imitated the West. He was a great critic whose social cartoons about the scenes and funny life of Kolkata and satire on Westernised Bengalis were popular. 'The Atrium' is a fine example of Cubist influence: a combination of geometrical shapes in various shades and tints with abstraction in the shapes.

la: Write an appreciative essay on Gaganendranath Tagore.

Gaganendranath Tagore (born 1867 in Kolkata, died 1938) was a leading figure of contemporary Indian painting. In 1910–21 he made sketches of the Himalayas, a sequence on the life of Chaitanya and drawings of Indian life. He supported his brother Abanindranath but inclined towards European Cubism and, after long experiment, developed his own brand: overlapping flattened geometrical shapes of colour create a mysterious world with a dramatic play of light and shade; he never blindly imitated the West. 'The Atrium' (1920, water colour on paper) is a fine example, composed of various shades and tints of geometrical shapes. He was also a great critic whose cartoons and satires on Westernised Bengalis were popular.
Review the evolution of Modern Indian Art.

Under British rule Indian art declined; miniatures and fresco were nearly lost and European oil painting and the Company School replaced them. Raja Ravi Varma bridged Indian subjects and western style. Abanindranath Tagore, Nandalal Bose and Benode Behari started the Bengal School at Santiniketan, taking subjects from Indian classics and mythology and rejecting western realism; Jamini Roy modernised folk art; Rabindranath Tagore added expression; Gaganendranath Tagore used cubist forms; Amrita Shergil blended Western training and Indian tradition. The Bengal School gave the starting point for contemporary Indian art.
Which European styles influenced Amrita Shergil most? What are the characteristics of the 'Brahmacharies' painting?

She studied in Paris and was influenced by Post-Impressionists like Modigliani and Gauguin, and she drew on Kangra miniatures and Ajanta frescoes. 'Brahmacharies' (1938, oil on canvas, National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi) shows five young Brahmin students as symbols of devotion, on a horizontal plane with vertical figures, a deep red background, subtle whites of dhotis and a neutral greenish-grey foreground giving calm.
